public_sources.title: Michael B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo Path Simulation, Operations Research 56(3), 2008
public_sources.observed_result: For a Lipschitz payoff with Euler discretisation, the paper proves that cost for O(epsilon) accuracy falls from O(epsilon^-3) for straightforward Monte Carlo to O(epsilon^-2 (log epsilon)^2) with multilevel Monte Carlo, using coupled coarse/fine corrections. This is a theorem for the stated SDE/discretisation conditions, not a universal factor speedup.

public_sources.title: Frederic Cerou and Arnaud Guyader, Adaptive Multilevel Splitting for Rare Event Analysis, 2007
public_sources.observed_result: The paper motivates splitting because naive Monte Carlo becomes unreasonable for probabilities below about 1e-9, and adapts the intermediate levels automatically. In the one-dimensional setting it proves consistency/asymptotic normality with the same asymptotic variance as fixed-level splitting while adding only small overhead relative to classical splitting.

public_sources.title: Riccardo Gozzo, Adaptive Multilevel Splitting: First Application to Rare-Event Derivative Pricing, arXiv:2510.23461v3
public_sources.observed_result: Version 3 was revised 2026-01-08. Across rare digital-option experiments under Black-Scholes/Heston settings, AMS reports gains up to 200-fold over standard Monte Carlo while preserving unbiasedness. The method adaptively kills low-score trajectories, clones better trajectories at their first crossing of the current level, and resimulates forward with fresh randomness. The paper explicitly notes that a score more aligned with the rare set reduces variance.

public_sources.title: Frederic Cerou, Patrick Heas, Mathias Rousset, Adaptive Reduced Multilevel Splitting, 2023
public_sources.observed_result: For rare events whose true score is expensive, the method uses an approximate surrogate score with certified error bounds and chooses critical levels adaptively from surrogate cost/error information. Numerical PDE experiments evaluate complexity versus squared error. No numeric speedup is imported here because the abstract-level evidence retrieved did not provide a single matched factor.

candidate_results.mechanism: When the quantity of interest is an extremely rare failure event in a restartable stochastic trajectory, stop spending nearly all evaluation budget on independent typical trajectories. Maintain a population, rank partial/complete trajectories by a progress score toward failure, kill the least advanced fraction, clone survivors at a crossed intermediate level, and resimulate only the suffix with fresh randomness. Use the AMS weight correction to estimate the rare-event probability rather than treating the enriched sample frequency as an unbiased raw frequency.
candidate_results.evidence: Foundational AMS theory targets regimes where crude MC is computationally unreasonable and gives adaptive-level asymptotic guarantees; a 2025/2026 finance implementation reports up to 200x computational gain over crude MC while retaining unbiasedness in its tested contracts.
candidate_results.transfer_hypothesis: For model/system evaluation, use this only for rare trajectory-level regressions or failures where simulator state can be cloned/restarted and a meaningful progress score exists. It could turn 'wait for a catastrophic failure by chance' into guided conditional search while still retaining a corrected probability estimator.
failure_conditions: A poor reaction coordinate/progress score can sharply reduce splitting efficiency even though admissible scoring can preserve unbiasedness.
The system must support valid branching/restart with fresh conditional randomness; irreversible real-world experiments do not automatically satisfy this.

Population cloning can reduce diversity if killing/resampling is too aggressive; the cited finance implementation recommends preserving enough survivors and finds runtime sensitive to the killing fraction.
The 200x figure is contract/model specific and cannot be generalized to AI evaluation without a matched experiment.

candidate_results.mechanism: For expectations or average metrics with a hierarchy of coupled evaluator fidelities, estimate the cheapest/coarsest level directly and estimate only adjacent fine-minus-coarse corrections at higher levels. Couple levels with the same underlying randomness so correction variance shrinks, and allocate many samples to cheap levels and progressively fewer to expensive levels.
candidate_results.evidence: Giles proves a complexity-order improvement from O(epsilon^-3) to O(epsilon^-2(log epsilon)^2) in the stated Euler/Lipschitz SDE setting.
candidate_results.transfer_hypothesis: For expensive research/evaluation loops, pair cheap proxy evaluators and expensive reference evaluators on identical seeds/scenarios, then estimate the expensive metric through telescoping corrections rather than treating proxy outputs as direct substitutes. This differs from transfer learning: the high-fidelity correction remains explicit rather than silently inheriting proxy bias.
failure_conditions: The gain relies on strong coarse/fine coupling and decay of correction variance. If fidelities disagree idiosyncratically, the multilevel advantage can collapse.
Discontinuous rare-event indicators can have slow correction-variance decay; rare failures may need splitting/importance methods instead of plain MLMC.
The Giles complexity theorem is scoped to assumptions on bias, variance decay and cost growth; it is not a blanket result for arbitrary evaluator ladders.

candidate_results.mechanism: Do not force one sampling strategy onto all evaluation questions. Route average/continuous metrics toward coupled multilevel corrections, and route ultra-rare trajectory failures toward adaptive splitting. If the rare-event score itself is expensive, investigate certified-surrogate splitting rather than using an uncertified proxy as ground truth.
candidate_results.status: derived synthesis; no direct end-to-end test

negative_or_scope_evidence: The AMS and MLMC gains arise in different mathematical regimes and should not be multiplied or presented as a combined speedup.
A rare-event score is a search/selection device, not automatically a calibrated failure probability; correct splitting weights or a valid estimator are required.
A low-fidelity evaluator is useful for MLMC only when paired differences are sufficiently low variance; high marginal correlation alone is not the full condition.
No claim is made that either mechanism improves AGI capability; these are candidate ways to spend evaluation/simulation budget more efficiently.
